name: V/A -(으)ㄴ/는/인 것 같다
briefDescription: Used to express a conjecture, guess, or a polite opinion based on observation.
featuredTranslation: It seems like it is raining.
longerExplanation: This structure is used when the speaker is making a guess based on external evidence or feelings. In Korean culture, it is also frequently used to express opinions indirectly or politely, even when the speaker is quite sure, to avoid sounding too blunt.

sentenceExamples.en: I think that person is a student.
It seems like the movie is interesting.
It looks like my friend was busy yesterday.

name: N보다
briefDescription: Used to compare two nouns, indicating the noun it is attached to is the standard of comparison.
featuredTranslation: This is bigger than that.
longerExplanation: The particle '보다' is attached directly to the noun that is being compared against (the baseline). In Korean word order, the thing you are comparing against usually comes before the adjective or verb of comparison.

sentenceExamples.en: Korean is more difficult than English.
Today is hotter than yesterday.
I like apples more than watermelons.

name: A/V-았/었으면 좋겠다
briefDescription: Expresses a desire or a hope for something to happen or a state to be achieved.
featuredTranslation: I wish break would come soon.
longerExplanation: This structure uses the past tense form (-았/었) followed by '으면 좋겠다'. While it literally translates to 'If [X] happened, it would be good,' it is the standard way to express 'I wish' or 'I hope' regardless of the actual timeframe.

sentenceExamples.en: I wish I had a lot of money.
I hope the weather is good tomorrow.
I wish I were a bit taller.

name: V-(으)ㄴ 적이 있다
briefDescription: Used to talk about past life experiences or something that has happened at least once.
featuredTranslation: I have been to Korea before.
longerExplanation: This structure focuses on whether an experience exists in one's past. To say you have 'never' done something, you replace '있다' with '없다' (V-(으)ㄴ 적이 없다). It is often paired with the 'V-아/어 보다' (try doing) form.

sentenceExamples.en: Have you ever tried eating Kimchi?
I have never seen that movie.
I have lived in Japan before.

name: V-면 되다
briefDescription: Indicates that a certain action is sufficient to satisfy a requirement or achieve a goal.
featuredTranslation: You only need to finish this.
longerExplanation: Literally 'If you do [X], it becomes [okay].' It is used to simplify instructions or to tell someone that they don't need to do more than what is specified.

sentenceExamples.en: Do I just need to sign here?
All you have to do is enter the password.
You just need to wait a little bit longer.

name: A/V -(으)ㄹ까요?
englishMeaning: Shall we V? / Do you think...?
briefDescription: Used to make a suggestion to the listener or to ask for the listener's opinion/conjecture about something.
featuredTranslation: Shall we go now?
longerExplanation: When the subject is 'we', it's a suggestion ('Shall we?'). When the subject is a third person or an event, it's asking for the listener's guess ('Do you think it will?').

sentenceExamples.en: Do you think it will rain tomorrow?
What shall we eat for lunch?
Do you think that person will like it?

name: A/V -(으)ㄹ 거예요
englishMeaning: I will V / It will A/V
briefDescription: Used to express a future plan, intention, or a strong prediction about a future event.
featuredTranslation: It will rain tomorrow.
longerExplanation: This is the most common way to express the future tense in Korean. With first-person subjects, it expresses intention ('I will'). With second or third-person subjects, it expresses a prediction or probability ('It likely will').

sentenceExamples.en: I'm going to meet a friend on the weekend.
The exam will probably be difficult.
I am going to study hard.

name: -아/어도
briefDescription: Used to show that the result is unaffected by the action. Similar to: -더라도 (No. 164).
featuredTranslation: No matter how busy I am, I still exercise.
longerExplanation: This is a concessive connector. It indicates that the condition in the first clause does not change or influence the situation in the second clause. It is frequently used with '아무리' (no matter how much).

sentenceExamples.en: Even if it rains, I will go.
No matter how much I eat, I'm still hungry.
Even if it's hard, don't give up.

name: -(으)ㄴ/는 대신에
briefDescription: Used to replace one action/noun with another. Similar to: -기보다 (No. 277).
featuredTranslation: I drink tea instead of coffee.
longerExplanation: This structure can be used with nouns (N 대신에) or verbs (V-는 대신에). It implies a substitution or a trade-off where one thing happens in place of another, or to compensate for another.

sentenceExamples.kr: 집을 청소하는 대신에 요리를 해 줄게요.
sentenceExamples.en: I'll cook for you instead of cleaning the house.
This laptop is expensive in exchange for being light.

sentenceExamples.kr: 영화관에 가는 대신에 집에서 영화를 봤어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Instead of going to the cinema, I watched a movie at home.

name: -(으)ㄴ/는 덕분에
briefDescription: Expresses a positive reason for a good result. Similar to: -아/어서 (No. 17) but strictly positive.
featuredTranslation: Thanks to my teacher, I passed.
longerExplanation: Unlike '-탓에' (blame), '-덕분에' is used only when the result is positive. It acknowledges a person, event, or state as the beneficial cause of the outcome.

sentenceExamples.kr: 날씨가 좋은 덕분에 소풍을 잘 다녀왔어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Thanks to the good weather, we had a nice picnic.

sentenceExamples.kr: 친구가 도와준 덕분에 일을 빨리 끝냈어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Thanks to my friend's help, I finished the work quickly.
I became healthy thanks to taking vitamins.

name: -고 나서
briefDescription: Emphasizes the completion of the first action before the second starts. Similar to: -은 후에 (No. 31).
featuredTranslation: After finishing your meal, please take the medicine.
longerExplanation: While '-고' simply means 'and', '-고 나서' clarifies that Action A must be completely finished before Action B begins. It provides a clearer chronological order.

sentenceExamples.kr: 숙제를 다 하고 나서 놀러 가세요.
sentenceExamples.en: Go play after you finish all your homework.

sentenceExamples.kr: 생각을 좀 하고 나서 대답해 줄래?
sentenceExamples.en: Can you answer me after you've thought about it for a bit?
After washing your hands, touch the food.

name: -(으)ㄴ/는데
briefDescription: Sets the background for a suggestion, question, or contrast. Similar to: -지만 (contrast).
featuredTranslation: The weather is good, (so) shall we go for a picnic?
longerExplanation: This is one of the most used connectors in Korean. It has three nuances: 1) Setting the stage for the next sentence. 2) Contrasting two facts. 3) Providing an explanation for why the speaker is asking something.

sentenceExamples.en: I am a student, but that person is a teacher (contrast).
I'm hungry, (so) let's go eat.
I watched a movie yesterday, but it was really boring.

name: -(으)려고
briefDescription: Expresses the subject's intention or purpose. Similar to: -(으)러 (No. 28).
featuredTranslation: I went to the cafe to meet a friend.
longerExplanation: Unlike '-(으)러' which only follows motion verbs like go/come, '-(으)려고' can be used with almost any action verb to show intent. You cannot use '-(으)세요' or '-(으)ㄹ까요' in the following clause.

sentenceExamples.en: I started exercising in order to lose weight.
I attend an academy to learn Korean.
I bought clothes intending to wear them tomorrow.

name: -아/어야
englishMeaning: Only if / Must... in order to
briefDescription: Indicates a strict prerequisite condition. Similar to: -(으)면 (No. 21) but stronger.
featuredTranslation: Only if you study hard can you pass.
longerExplanation: This structure emphasizes that the first clause is an absolute necessity. Without Action A, Action B is impossible. It is the basis for '-아/어야 하다' (must do).

sentenceExamples.en: Only if you try it yourself will you know the taste.
Only if you have money can you go on a trip, right?

sentenceExamples.kr: 키가 커야 농구 선수가 될 수 있어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Only if you are tall can you become a basketball player.

name: -거나
briefDescription: Used to list choices between verbs or adjectives. Similar to: -(이)나 (No. 69).
featuredTranslation: On weekends, I either read books or sleep.
longerExplanation: Used when connecting two or more actions or states where only one is chosen or happens. For nouns, you use '-(이)나', but for verbs/adjectives, you use '-거나'.

sentenceExamples.en: If you are busy or having a hard time, please tell me.
In the morning, I either eat bread or drink milk.

sentenceExamples.kr: 노래를 듣거나 영화를 보는 것을 좋아해요.
sentenceExamples.en: I like either listening to music or watching movies.

name: -(으)ㄹ수록
briefDescription: Shows that the degree of the second clause increases in proportion to the first. Similar to: -면 -수록 (combined form).
featuredTranslation: The more I study Korean, the harder it gets.
longerExplanation: This structure indicates a proportional relationship. Often paired with '-면' (e.g., 보면 볼수록 - the more I look at it, the more...) to emphasize the effect.

sentenceExamples.en: The more people, the better.
The cheaper the item, the better it sells.
The more (rice) ripens, the more it bows its head (humility proverb).

name: -아/어서
briefDescription: Expresses a reason or a chronological sequence. Similar to: -(으)니까 (No. 20) for reasons.
featuredTranslation: Because my stomach hurt, I went to the hospital.
longerExplanation: This has two distinct roles: 1) Cause/Reason: providing a basic reason. 2) Time sequence: Action A happened, and *because* of that state, Action B followed (usually with closely related actions). You cannot use commands or suggestions with '-아/어서'.

sentenceExamples.en: I'm tired because I slept late yesterday.
I met my friend and then (we) watched a movie.
I was late because the roads were blocked.

name: -아/어서 그런지
briefDescription: Used to give a reason that the speaker is not 100% sure about. Similar to: -아/어서 (No. 17).
featuredExample: 어제 잠을 못 자서 그런지 피곤하네요.
featuredTranslation: Maybe because I couldn't sleep yesterday, I feel tired.
longerExplanation: This adds a layer of conjecture to a reason. Use this when you are guessing that [X] is the reason for [Y], but you aren't stating it as an absolute fact.

sentenceExamples.kr: 날씨가 추워서 그런지 감기 환자가 많아요.
sentenceExamples.en: Perhaps because the weather is cold, there are many cold patients.
Maybe because it's Monday, the traffic is very heavy.

sentenceExamples.kr: 기분이 좋아서 그런지 음식이 더 맛있어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Perhaps because I'm in a good mood, the food tastes even better.

name: -(으)면서
briefDescription: Indicates two actions happening at the exact same time by the same person. Similar to: -는 동안 (No. 32).
featuredTranslation: I study while listening to music.
longerExplanation: The subject for both actions must be the same. It is used to describe multi-tasking or two states existing concurrently.

sentenceExamples.en: I watch TV while eating a meal.
Don't talk on the phone while driving.
That person laughed while crying.

name: -(으)니까
briefDescription: Expresses a subjective reason or a discovery. Similar to: -아/어서 (No. 17).
featuredTranslation: Since it's raining, take an umbrella.
longerExplanation: Differences from '-아/어서': 1) It can be used with commands (-으세요) and suggestions (-ㄹ까요). 2) It expresses a more subjective or speaker-centered reason. 3) It can mean 'when I did [X], I found out [Y]'.

sentenceExamples.kr: 내가 해 보니까 별로 안 어려워요.
sentenceExamples.en: Now that I've tried it, it's not that hard.
Since we're hungry, let's eat quickly.
Since it's cold, please close the window.

name: -(으)면
briefDescription: Used for general conditions or hypothetical situations. Similar to: -다면 (No. 289).
featuredTranslation: If you have time, shall we watch a movie together?
longerExplanation: This is the most basic conditional. It can describe a simple 'if' (hypothetical) or a repetitive 'when' (whenever something happens).

sentenceExamples.kr: 비가 오면 소풍을 안 갈 거예요.
sentenceExamples.en: If it rains, we won't go on a picnic.
When you come to Korea, please make sure to contact me.
If you study hard, you can pass.

name: -게
englishMeaning: So that / In a way that
briefDescription: Expresses a purpose or an adverbial form. Similar to: -도록 (No. 117).
featuredTranslation: Please be quiet so that my sibling can sleep.
longerExplanation: 1) Purpose: similar to 'in order to'. 2) Adverbializer: turns adjectives into adverbs (e.g., '예쁘게' - beautifully). In your textbook image, it is listed as a 'purpose' grammar.

sentenceExamples.en: I will explain it to you in an easy way (easily).
Speak loudly so that the person in the back can hear too.
I cut my hair short.

name: -고
briefDescription: Basic connector for listing or chronological sequence. Similar to: -아/어서 (No. 17).
featuredExample: 저는 사과를 먹고 친구는 빵을 먹어요.
featuredTranslation: I am eating an apple, and my friend is eating bread.
longerExplanation: The most fundamental connector. Use it to list two facts (Action A and Action B) or to show Action A happened first, followed by Action B. Unlike '-아/어서', the first and second clauses don't need a causal link.

sentenceExamples.en: I did my homework and then played games.
Yesterday was hot, and today is cool.
I like bibimbap, and I like kimchi too.

name: -아/어 주다
briefDescription: Indicates that an action is performed as a favor or service for another. Similar to: -아/어 드리다 (honorific).
featuredTranslation: Please open the door (for me).
longerExplanation: This adds a nuance of 'help' or 'favor' to a verb. To make it polite/honorific toward the person you are helping, you use '-아/어 드리다'. To make a request, you use '-아/어 주세요'.

sentenceExamples.en: Shall I carry your bag for you?
Please take a photo for me.
My friend bought a birthday present for me.

name: -아/어야 하다
briefDescription: Expresses obligation or necessity. Similar to: -아/어야 되다.
featuredTranslation: I have to wake up early tomorrow.
longerExplanation: This is based on the condition '-아/어야' (only if). Literally: 'Only if I wake up early, is it okay.' Both '-해야 하다' and '-해야 되다' are common, though '-하다' is slightly more formal.

sentenceExamples.en: You must exercise for your health.
You must keep the appointment time.
Where do I have to get off?

name: -기 때문에
briefDescription: A clear, logical reason. Similar to: -아/어서 (No. 17).
featuredTranslation: Because it's snowing, the roads are slippery.
longerExplanation: This is a much stronger and clearer reason than '-아/어서'. It is common in writing and formal speech. Like '-아/어서', it cannot be used with commands or suggestions.

sentenceExamples.en: Because it's exam period, I'm busy.
I didn't buy it because it's too expensive.
I went to the hospital because I caught a cold.

name: -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다
briefDescription: Expresses the ability or the possibility of doing something. Similar to: -지 못하다 (cannot).
featuredTranslation: I can speak Korean.
longerExplanation: This structure covers both 'ability' (I know how to) and 'possibility' (It is possible to). It is one of the first structures learned by beginners.

sentenceExamples.en: You cannot take photos here.
Can you eat spicy food?
I can drive, but I don't have a car.

name: -(으)러 (가다/오다)
briefDescription: Shows the purpose of going or coming to a place. Similar to: -(으)려고 (No. 13).
featuredTranslation: I'm going to the cinema to watch a movie.
longerExplanation: Strict grammar rule: The second clause must contain a motion verb like '가다' (go), '오다' (come), or '다니다' (attend/commute). For general purposes, use '-(으)려고'.

sentenceExamples.en: I came to the restaurant to eat.
I'm going to the cafe to meet a friend.
I'm going to the library to study.

name: -지 마세요
briefDescription: The negative command form. Similar to: -지 마 (informal).
featuredTranslation: Please don't worry.
longerExplanation: Used when telling someone to stop or not perform an action. It is the polite negative version of '-(으)세요'.

sentenceExamples.en: Please don't smoke here.
Please don't eat too much.
Please don't give up.

name: -아/어 놓다
englishMeaning: V and keep it that way
briefDescription: Completion and maintenance of a state. Similar to: -아/어 두다 (No. 82).
featuredTranslation: I opened the window (and kept it open).
longerExplanation: Used when an action is performed and the result is kept for a period of time, often in preparation for something else. Note: '놓다' is usually for shorter preparation, '두다' for longer storage.

sentenceExamples.en: I have made a reservation in advance.
I will have the food ready (and keep it that way).
Please write down your name (so it stays there).

name: -(으)ㄴ 후에 / 뒤에
briefDescription: Indicates Action B happens after Action A is finished. Similar to: -고 나서 (No. 11).
featuredTranslation: Let's meet after the class finishes.
longerExplanation: This is the standard 'after' structure. It is attached to the past noun form of a verb. It is slightly more formal than '-고 나서' and is used in both speaking and writing to show chronological order.

sentenceExamples.en: Please eat after washing your hands.
After watching the movie, we drank coffee.
I want to get a job after graduating.

name: -는 동안
briefDescription: Indicates the duration of an action. Similar to: -(으)면서 (No. 19).
featuredTranslation: I read a book while waiting for my friend.
longerExplanation: Unlike '-(으)면서', which requires the same subject for both actions, '-는 동안' can have different subjects in each clause. It focuses purely on the time interval in which an action takes place.

sentenceExamples.kr: 엄마가 요리하는 동안 저는 청소를 했어요.
sentenceExamples.en: While my mom was cooking, I did the cleaning.
I will go on a trip during the vacation.
Don't look at your phone while you are studying.

name: -기 전에
briefDescription: Indicates Action B happens before Action A. Similar to: -(으)ㄴ 후에 (No. 31) [Opposite].
featuredTranslation: I brush my teeth before sleeping.
longerExplanation: Attached to the verb stem, '-기 전에' creates the meaning of 'before.' It can be used with both verbs and nouns (N 전에). It is a foundational Level 1 structure essential for daily routines.

sentenceExamples.en: Wash your hands before eating.
I arrived before the movie started.

sentenceExamples.kr: 결혼하기 전에 세계 여행을 하고 싶어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I want to travel the world before getting married.

name: -고 싶다
briefDescription: Expresses the speaker's desire. Similar to: -(으)면 좋겠다 (No. 3).
featuredTranslation: I want to go to Korea.
longerExplanation: Used for first-person desires. For third-person desires ('He/She wants to'), you must use '-고 싶어 하다'. This is one of the most basic expressions of will or wish in the Korean language.

sentenceExamples.en: I want to eat Bibimbap.
I listen to music when I want to rest.
What kind of gift do you want to receive?

name: -아/어 보다
englishMeaning: Try doing V / Have tried V
briefDescription: Expresses trying something or having an experience. Similar to: -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다 (No. 4).
featuredTranslation: Please try on these clothes.
longerExplanation: In the present/imperative, it means 'try doing.' In the past tense (-아/어 봤다), it expresses experience ('I have tried'). It is used to encourage others to attempt an action.

sentenceExamples.en: I have tried Korean food.
I want to try going to Jeju Island.
Please try reading this book once.

name: -아/어지다
briefDescription: Expresses a change in state for adjectives. Similar to: -게 되다 (No. 85).
featuredTranslation: The weather became cold (got colder).
longerExplanation: This turns adjectives into a process of change. '예쁘다' (to be pretty) becomes '예뻐지다' (to become pretty). It is frequently used to compare the current state with a previous state.

sentenceExamples.kr: 공부를 열심히 해서 한국어 실력이 좋아졌어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Because I studied hard, my Korean skills became better.
The room has become clean.
It is gradually becoming hotter.

name: -기 시작하다
briefDescription: Indicates the beginning of an action. Similar to: -게 되다 (No. 85).
featuredTranslation: It started to rain.
longerExplanation: Used when an action or a natural phenomenon commences. It is simply the verb 'start' attached to a nominalized verb stem.

sentenceExamples.en: I started learning Korean last month.
The baby started to walk.
I will start exercising from tomorrow.

name: -기 쉽다 / 어렵다
briefDescription: Expresses the ease or difficulty of performing an action. Similar to: -(으)ㄹ 만하다 (No. 108).
featuredTranslation: This book is easy to read.
longerExplanation: By attaching '-기' to the verb stem, the action becomes a noun, which is then described as easy or difficult. This is common when giving reviews or instructions.

sentenceExamples.en: The road is slippery, so it's easy to fall.
This word is hard to memorize.
I'm looking for a phone that is easy to use.

name: -(으)ㄴ/는 것
briefDescription: Turns a verb into a noun to be used as a subject or object. Similar to: -기.
featuredTranslation: I like exercising.
longerExplanation: This is the most common way to talk about hobbies or activities. It allows you to use a verb in positions where only a noun can normally go, such as before '좋아하다' (like).

sentenceExamples.en: My hobby is cooking.
Watching Korean dramas is fun.
I enjoy traveling alone.

name: -(으)ㄹ 때
briefDescription: Indicates the time when a certain action or state occurs. Similar to: -는 동안 (No. 32).
featuredTranslation: I received a call when I was eating.
longerExplanation: This is used for specific points in time or general situations. It can be used with past, present, or future contexts depending on the tense of the following clause.

sentenceExamples.en: What do you do when you have time?
When I was young, I was very small.
Take this medicine when you are tired.

name: -지요? (-죠?)
briefDescription: Used to confirm something with the listener. Similar to: -지? (informal).
featuredTranslation: The weather is cold today, right?
longerExplanation: Used when the speaker already has a guess or knowledge about a fact and wants the listener to agree or confirm. It is polite but friendly.

sentenceExamples.en: You like Korean food, don't you?
We're meeting tomorrow, right?
This is correct, right?

name: -고 있다
briefDescription: Indicates an action currently in progress. Similar to: -는 중이다 (in the middle of).
featuredTranslation: I am waiting for a friend right now.
longerExplanation: This is the present progressive form. It emphasizes that the action is happening at the very moment of speaking. It can also describe a continuous state if used with verbs like wearing clothes.

sentenceExamples.en: I am listening to a song.
My younger sibling is doing homework.
He is wearing glasses (state of wearing).

name: N이에요/예요
briefDescription: The basic polite ending used to identify or define a noun. Similar to: N입니다 (No. 44).
featuredTranslation: I am a student.
longerExplanation: Used to attach 'to be' to a noun in a polite, informal setting. '이에요' is used after a consonant (받침), and '예요' is used after a vowel.

sentenceExamples.en: This is my bag.
My friend is a chef.
Tomorrow is my birthday.

name: N입니다 / N입니까?
briefDescription: The formal version of the verb 'to be'. Similar to: N이에요/예요 (No. 43).
featuredTranslation: Nice to meet you. I am Kim Min-su.
longerExplanation: Used in formal situations like introductions, news, or business. '입니다' is the statement form, and '입니까?' is the question form.

sentenceExamples.en: What is your occupation?
This is Seoul Station.
That person is our teacher.

name: N이/가 아닙니다
briefDescription: The formal negation of 'to be'. Similar to: N이/가 아니에요.
featuredTranslation: I am not Japanese.
longerExplanation: Used to state that the subject is not the noun mentioned. Requires the subject particle '이/가' attached to the noun.

sentenceExamples.en: This is not my wallet.
Today is not a holiday.
That person is not a doctor.

name: N이/가 있어요/없어요
englishMeaning: To have / To exist / There is
briefDescription: Used to express possession or the existence of a noun in a location.
featuredTranslation: I have a Korean friend.
longerExplanation: Used to say 'I have [N]' or 'There is [N]'. If the noun ends in a consonant, use '이', if a vowel, use '가'.

sentenceExamples.en: The teacher is in the classroom.
I don't have an umbrella.
Do you have time?

name: N 주세요
briefDescription: A basic polite way to request a noun (items/food). Similar to: V-아/어 주세요 (Requesting an action).
featuredTranslation: Please give me some water.
longerExplanation: The standard way to order food or ask for an item in a shop. It combines the noun with '주다' (to give) in the polite imperative form.

sentenceExamples.en: Please give me the menu.
Please give me one roll of kimbap.
Please give me three apples.

name: N하고, N과/와
briefDescription: Used to connect two nouns. Similar to: N(이)랑 (colloquial).
featuredTranslation: I ate bread and milk.
longerExplanation: '하고' is common in speech. '과/와' is slightly more formal; '과' follows a consonant, '와' follows a vowel.

sentenceExamples.en: I watched a movie with a friend yesterday.
There are desks and chairs in the classroom.
My sibling and I are very different.

name: V-아요/어요
briefDescription: The standard polite present tense ending for verbs and adjectives.
featuredTranslation: I am going home now.
longerExplanation: Used to describe current actions or general facts. If the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, use '-아요'. For all other vowels, use '-어요'. 하요 becomes 해요.

sentenceExamples.en: I am eating lunch.
The weather is good today.
I study Korean every day.

name: N에서
briefDescription: Indicates the place where an action occurs. Similar to: N에 (Location of existence).
featuredTranslation: I study at the library.
longerExplanation: Unlike '에', which marks where something *is*, '에서' marks where something *happens*.

sentenceExamples.en: I meet a friend at a restaurant.
I bought clothes at the department store.
I am resting at home.

name: 안 V
briefDescription: The short form of negation. Similar to: -지 않다.
featuredTranslation: I don't eat meat.
longerExplanation: Placing '안' before a verb or adjective makes it negative. For 'Noun+하다' verbs, '안' goes between the noun and '하다' (e.g., 공부 안 해요).

sentenceExamples.en: I am not going to school today.
The movie is not interesting.
I was tired, so I didn't do my homework.

name: N에 (Destination)
briefDescription: Used with motion verbs (go, come) to indicate the destination.
featuredTranslation: I go to the mountain on the weekend.
longerExplanation: Attached to a location noun when used with verbs like 가다, 오다, 다니다.

sentenceExamples.en: When are you coming to Korea?
I go to the office (commute) every day.
Where do you want to go?

name: N 앞, 뒤, 옆, 위, 밑
englishMeaning: In front, Behind, Beside, On, Under
briefDescription: Spatial nouns used to indicate precise location. Similar to: N 근처 (Nearby).
featuredTranslation: There is a convenience store in front of the school.
longerExplanation: These nouns specify position and are almost always followed by the location particle '에'.

sentenceExamples.en: The book is on the desk.
There is a pharmacy beside the bank.
The puppy is sleeping under the bed.

name: N에 (Time)
briefDescription: Indicates the time when a certain action or state occurs. Similar to: -ㄹ 때 (No. 40).
featuredTranslation: I wake up at 8 AM.
longerExplanation: Attached to nouns of time like hours, days, months, and years. (Note: Do not use with 'today', 'tomorrow', or 'yesterday').

sentenceExamples.en: I will meet a friend on Sunday.
My birthday is in December.
I can't sleep at night.

name: N 개, 번, 명, 권
briefDescription: Nouns used with Native Korean numbers to count items.
featuredTranslation: Give me two apples, please.
longerExplanation: Korean uses specific counters for different objects. 개 (items), 번 (times), 명 (people), 권 (books), 병 (bottles), 잔 (glasses/cups).

sentenceExamples.en: There are four people in my family.
I want to drink a cup of coffee.
I read this book three times.

name: N도
briefDescription: Used to add the meaning of 'also' to a noun.
featuredTranslation: I like apples and I also like bananas.
longerExplanation: Replaces particles like 이/가 or 을/를 to indicate that the noun is being added to a previous statement.

sentenceExamples.en: I am a student too.
Are you busy tomorrow too?
I can also speak Korean.

name: A/V-습니다 / ㅂ니다
briefDescription: The standard ending for formal and official contexts. Similar to: -아요/어요 (No. 49).
featuredTranslation: I study hard (Formal).
longerExplanation: Used in the military, business, news, and when addressing a large public audience. It conveys maximum respect and social distance.

sentenceExamples.en: The weather is hot (Formal).
What are you looking for? (Formal)
The food is very delicious (Formal).

name: A/V-네요
briefDescription: Used to express surprise or realization upon discovering a fact.
featuredTranslation: The baby is so cute!
longerExplanation: Used when you personally see, feel, or experience something for the first time and want to exclaim about it. It’s like saying 'Wow, it's really [X]!'

sentenceExamples.en: You speak Korean quite well!
Wow, it's already 12 o'clock.
Look, it's snowing.

name: N(의) N
briefDescription: Indicates that the second noun belongs to or is related to the first noun.
featuredTranslation: This is my book.
longerExplanation: Attached to a noun to show possession. In speech, '나의' becomes '내', '저의' becomes '제', and '너의' becomes '네'. The particle '의' is often pronounced as '에'.

sentenceExamples.en: Do you know your friend's phone number?
Our country's history is deep.
Whose bag is this?

name: N을/를 잘하다 / 못하다
briefDescription: Used to express one's skill level in a specific area/activity.
featuredTranslation: I am good at swimming.
longerExplanation: Well-known phrases to describe ability. '잘하다' means to be skillful, while '못하다' means to be unskillful or unable.

sentenceExamples.en: I am not good at Korean.
My younger sibling is good at cooking.
I want to be good at singing.

name: A/V-(으)시-
briefDescription: Inserted into verbs/adjectives to show respect to the person performing the action.
featuredTranslation: The teacher is reading the newspaper.
longerExplanation: This is a fundamental part of Korean politeness. Use it when the subject of the sentence (the person doing the action) is someone of higher status than you (like a boss, teacher, or elder).

sentenceExamples.en: My mother is sleeping now.
Where did your father go?
What are you doing? (Honorific/Formal)

name: N부터 N까지
briefDescription: Indicates the starting and ending points of a period of time.
featuredTranslation: I work from 9 o'clock to 6 o'clock.
longerExplanation: '부터' marks the start time, and '까지' marks the end time. Similar to N에서 N까지 (No. 63) which is for distance.

sentenceExamples.en: From what time did you study yesterday?
Lunch time is from 12 to 1.
I go to school from Monday to Friday.

name: N에서 N까지
briefDescription: Indicates the starting and ending points of a physical range or distance.
featuredTranslation: I go from Seoul to Busan by train.
longerExplanation: Used to describe travel or distance. '에서' is the starting location, '까지' is the destination.

sentenceExamples.en: How long does it take from home to school?
Run from here to there.
I go from Incheon to Paris by plane.

name: N(으)로 (Direction / Means)
briefDescription: Indicates the direction toward a place or the tool/method used.
featuredTranslation: Please go to the left.
longerExplanation: Has two main uses: 1) Direction (go toward). 2) Method/Tool (go *by* bus, write *with* a pen).

sentenceExamples.en: It takes 30 minutes by bus.
Please write your name with a pencil.
Please speak in Korean (via the means of Korean).

name: A-(으)ㄴ N
briefDescription: Used to turn an adjective into a descriptive word that comes before a noun. (e.g., 'A pretty girl').
featuredTranslation: I want to eat delicious food.
longerExplanation: To describe a noun, you attach '-(으)ㄴ' to the adjective stem. '크다' becomes '큰', '작다' becomes '작은'.

sentenceExamples.en: I bought pretty clothes.
Do you know a quiet cafe?
Please give me some cool water.

name: N한테 / N께 / N에게
briefDescription: Indicates the recipient of an action. '께' is the honorific version.
featuredTranslation: I am writing a letter to a friend.
longerExplanation: '한테' is most common in speech. '에게' is more formal/written. '께' is used for someone you must respect (like a teacher or grandmother).

sentenceExamples.en: I asked the teacher a question.
I gave food to the dog.
I contacted my parents (Formal/Written).

name: V-(으)ㄹ게요
briefDescription: Used to express a promise or an intention to the listener. Similar to: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (No. 7).
featuredTranslation: I will call you again tomorrow (I promise).
longerExplanation: Unlike '-ㄹ 거예요' (a general future prediction), '-ㄹ게요' is a commitment made directly to the person you are talking to. It can only be used with first-person subjects ('I' or 'We').

sentenceExamples.en: I will help you.
I won't forget (I promise).
I will go later so that I'm not late.

name: V-는 N
briefDescription: Turns a verb into a description for a noun in the present tense. (e.g., 'The person who is studying').
featuredTranslation: The book I am reading right now is interesting.
longerExplanation: Attaching '-는' to a verb stem allows it to describe the noun that follows. It focuses on the action currently in progress.

sentenceExamples.kr: 저기 춤을 추는 사람이 제 친구예요.
sentenceExamples.en: The person dancing over there is my friend.
What is the food that you like?
I have many friends who go to (work at) companies.

name: N(이)나 (Or)
briefDescription: Used to list options between two or more nouns. Similar to: -거나 (No. 15).
featuredTranslation: Shall we drink coffee or tea?
longerExplanation: Attached to the first noun to suggest a choice. If the noun ends in a consonant, use '이나'; if it ends in a vowel, use '나'.

sentenceExamples.en: Shall we watch a movie or something this weekend?
In the morning, I eat bread or kimbap.
If you're bored, read a comic book or something.

name: V-(으)ㄴ N
briefDescription: Describes a noun based on a completed action. (e.g., 'The book I read').
featuredTranslation: This is the movie I watched yesterday.
longerExplanation: Attaching '-(으)ㄴ' to a verb stem describes a noun that was the object of a finished action.

sentenceExamples.kr: 이미 간 사람은 어쩔 수 없어요.
sentenceExamples.en: There is nothing we can do about the person who already left.
Do you remember the words I said earlier?
I wore the clothes I bought yesterday.

name: V-(으)ㄹ N
briefDescription: Describes a noun based on an action that will happen in the future. (e.g., 'The place I will go').
featuredTranslation: There are a lot of things to do tomorrow.
longerExplanation: Attaching '-(으)ㄹ' to a verb stem describes a noun in terms of future plans or prospects.

sentenceExamples.en: I am preparing the food to eat this evening.
Have you decided on the place to go during the break?
There is a lot of content to study for this exam.

name: N처럼
briefDescription: Used to compare two things by saying one is like the other. Similar to: -듯이 (No. 111).
featuredTranslation: You sing well like a singer.
longerExplanation: Direct comparison. It implies the subject shares the characteristics or qualities of the noun.

sentenceExamples.en: My friend is kind like an angel.
Today is hot like summer.
You are tall like a model.

name: N마다
briefDescription: Attached to time or object nouns to mean 'every' or 'without exception'.
featuredTranslation: I go hiking every weekend.
longerExplanation: Expresses repetition or universality across a category. (e.g., 나라마다 - every country).

sentenceExamples.en: Every person has a different personality.
There are many people at every bus stop.
I go jogging every morning.

name: V-는 게 어때요?
briefDescription: A polite way to make a suggestion. Similar to: V-지 그래요? (No. 242).
featuredTranslation: How about eating lunch together?
longerExplanation: Used to give advice or propose a plan politely. It literally means 'How is the act of [V]?'

sentenceExamples.en: How about resting for a moment?

sentenceExamples.kr: 다른 옷을 입어 보는 게 어때요?
sentenceExamples.en: How about trying on different clothes?

sentenceExamples.kr: 이 책을 읽는 게 어때요? 진짜 재미있어요.
sentenceExamples.en: How about reading this book? It's really fun.

name: N 중에(서)
briefDescription: Indicates a range or group from which a choice is made.
featuredTranslation: Among fruits, I like apples the most.
longerExplanation: Used when selecting one or more items from a set. Can also be used with time (e.g., 수업 중에 - in the middle of class).

sentenceExamples.kr: 우리 반 중에서 누가 제일 커요?
sentenceExamples.en: Who is the tallest among our class?
Please choose one between the two.

sentenceExamples.kr: 지금 회의 중이라서 전화를 못 받아요.
sentenceExamples.en: I'm in the middle of a meeting, so I can't pick up the phone.

name: V-(으)ㄹ래(요)
englishMeaning: I want to / Would you like to? (Intention)
briefDescription: Used to express the speaker's will or to ask about the listener's preference.
featuredTranslation: I want to eat Bibimbap.
longerExplanation: A casual but polite way to state an intent or make a proposal. Often used when ordering food or deciding on a plan with friends.

sentenceExamples.en: Would you like to drink coffee?
Do you want to watch a movie together this weekend?
I'll just rest at home.

name: N밖에
briefDescription: Used to emphasize that the quantity or option is smaller than expected. Must be followed by a negative ending.
featuredTranslation: There is only one student in the classroom.
longerExplanation: Focuses on the lack of other options. Unlike '만' (only), '밖에' always requires a negative verb like '없다', '모르다', or '안 하다'.

sentenceExamples.en: I have only 1,000 won left (nothing but 1,000 won).
No one but me knows that news.
I've only waited for 10 minutes.

name: N(이)라서
briefDescription: The noun form of the reason connector -아서/어서.
featuredTranslation: I feel good because today is my birthday.
longerExplanation: Attached to a noun to give it a causal meaning. Use '이라서' after a consonant and '라서' after a vowel.

sentenceExamples.en: Because this is a quiet place, it's good for studying.
Because I'm a student, I don't have much money.
Because it's the weekend, there are many people at the department store.

name: N(이)나 (Emphasis/Quantity)
englishMeaning: As many as / No less than
briefDescription: Used to express that an amount or quantity is larger than the speaker expected.
featuredTranslation: I drank as many as five cups of coffee.
longerExplanation: When attached to a number or counter, it adds a nuance of surprise or emphasis on the scale of the quantity.

sentenceExamples.en: I bought no less than 10 apples.
It takes as much as an hour from home to school.
Wow, it's already 3 o'clock (later than I thought).

name: A/V-았을/었을 때
briefDescription: Indicates the time when a past action or state occurred.
featuredExample: 한국에 처음 왔을 때 김치를 못 먹었어요.
featuredTranslation: When I first came to Korea, I couldn't eat Kimchi.
longerExplanation: Combines the past tense '-았/었' with '-을 때'. Used to set the timeframe for a past memory or event.

sentenceExamples.en: When I was young, I was very small.
I was really happy when I graduated from university.
When I got lost, a police officer helped me.

name: V-는 셈이다
englishMeaning: It's virtually V / Practically the same as...
briefDescription: Used when a situation is not exactly as stated, but the result or effect is almost identical.
featuredTranslation: Since I lived there 10 years, it's virtually my hometown.
longerExplanation: This is a 'calculation' or 'conclusion' grammar. After considering all the facts, the speaker concludes that the current situation is effectively equivalent to something else. '셈' refers to a calculation or an account.

sentenceExamples.kr: 거의 다 했으니 다 끝난 셈이에요.
sentenceExamples.en: I'm almost done, so it's practically finished.
It's so cheap it's practically free.

sentenceExamples.kr: 비긴 것이나 마찬가지니까 우리가 이긴 셈이에요.
sentenceExamples.en: It's the same as a tie, so we've basically won.

name: V-아/어 놓다 / 두다
briefDescription: Indicates that an action has been completed and the resulting state is maintained for future use.
featuredTranslation: I opened the door and left it open.
longerExplanation: Both '놓다' and '두다' indicate performing an action and then leaving it that way. '놓다' often implies the action was done in preparation for something else, while '두다' can imply keeping something in a certain place or state for a longer period.

sentenceExamples.en: I made a reservation in advance (and it's set).
I finished all my homework and kept it ready.
I will prepare the food (so it's ready when you come).

name: V-기로 하다
briefDescription: Used to express a promise to oneself (resolution) or an agreement with others.
featuredTranslation: I decided to exercise every day.
longerExplanation: This structure turns the verb into a noun clause with '-기' and follows with '하다' (to do). It is usually used in the past tense '했다' to show that the decision or promise has already been made.

sentenceExamples.en: I agreed to meet my friend at 6 o'clock.
I decided to quit smoking this year.
Let's agree to talk again tomorrow.

name: V-게 하다
briefDescription: Indicates that the subject makes or allows another person to perform an action.
featuredTranslation: I made my younger sibling clean.
longerExplanation: This is the causative form. It can mean either 'force/order' someone to do something or 'allow/permit' them to do it, depending on the context. '게' acts as an adverbializer for the verb.

sentenceExamples.en: The teacher made the students laugh.

sentenceExamples.kr: 부모님은 제가 유학을 가게 해 주셨어요.
sentenceExamples.en: My parents let me go study abroad.
Please make the child go to sleep early.

name: V-게 되다
englishMeaning: Came to be V / Ended up V-ing
briefDescription: Expresses a change in state or a result that happened due to external circumstances, not necessarily the subject's will.
featuredTranslation: I came to work at this company.
longerExplanation: While '-아/어지다' is used for adjectives (becoming pretty), '-게 되다' is used for verbs. It implies that a situation developed or a decision was made by factors outside the person's direct control.

sentenceExamples.en: It's been decided that I'm moving next month.
I wore glasses, so I can see well now (it became so).
How did you end up coming to Korea?

name: V-아/어 있다
englishMeaning: Is in the state of V-ing (Resulting state)
briefDescription: Used to describe a continuing state that results from a completed action.
featuredTranslation: The flower is blooming (state).
longerExplanation: Unlike '-고 있다' which describes an action currently in progress, '-아/어 있다' describes the state that remains after the action is finished. It is typically used with intransitive verbs (verbs that don't take an object) like sitting, standing, blooming, or opening.

sentenceExamples.en: I am sitting on the chair (in the state of having sat down).
The door is open (it was opened and remains so).
A picture is hanging on the wall.

name: V-아/어 가다
englishMeaning: Is continuing toward V / Finishing up
briefDescription: Indicates that an action is currently in progress and moving toward completion or the future.
featuredTranslation: I am finishing up the homework.
longerExplanation: This structure expresses that an action is 'going along' toward a finish line. It implies the process is almost done or is steadily progressing away from the current moment into the future.

sentenceExamples.en: The preparations are almost finished.
The children are growing up well.

sentenceExamples.kr: 음식이 다 되어 가니까 조금만 기다리세요.
sentenceExamples.en: The food is almost ready, so please wait a bit.

name: V-아/어 오다
briefDescription: Indicates that an action started in the past and has continued steadily up until the present.
featuredTranslation: I have been studying Korean for 5 years.
longerExplanation: This is the counterpart to 'V-아/어 가다'. While '가다' looks toward the future, '오다' looks back at the past, emphasizing the continuity of an action from then until now.

sentenceExamples.en: He has lived honestly until now.
We have been waiting for a long time.
We have been keeping the tradition alive.

name: V-(으)ㄹ 뻔했다
briefDescription: Used to describe a situation where something almost happened but ultimately did not.
featuredTranslation: I almost fell down.
longerExplanation: This structure is used to express relief or surprise about a 'near miss.' It is often used with the adverb '하마터면' (meaning 'nearly' or 'by a hair's breadth') to add emphasis to the danger or closeness of the event.

sentenceExamples.en: An accident almost happened.
I was so surprised I almost cried.
I almost missed the bus.

name: V/A/N-나 보다
briefDescription: Expresses a guess based on something the speaker has seen or heard.
featuredTranslation: I guess the weather is cold.
longerExplanation: This is used when you make a conjecture based on external evidence. For example, if you see people outside wearing heavy coats, you might say '날씨가 춥나 봐요'. It is generally used for present tense guesses.

sentenceExamples.kr: 사람들이 많은 걸 보니 맛집인가 봐요.
sentenceExamples.en: Seeing as there are many people, I guess it's a famous restaurant.
I guess that person is very busy.
I guess they couldn't sleep yesterday.

name: V/A-ㄴ/는 모양이다
briefDescription: Expresses a strong conjecture based on specific evidence or a certain situation. Similar to: -나 보다 (No. 90).
featuredTranslation: It appears that he has already arrived.
longerExplanation: Similar to '-나 보다', but '-ㄴ/는 모양이다' implies a more logical deduction based on factual evidence. '모양' literally means 'shape' or 'appearance,' so you are saying 'it takes the shape/appearance of [X] happening.'

sentenceExamples.kr: 불이 꺼진 걸 보니 집에 없는 모양이에요.
sentenceExamples.en: Seeing the lights are off, it appears they are not home.
It looks like those two had a fight.
It appears that the preparation is not done yet.

name: V-아/어 버렸다
briefDescription: Indicates that an action is completely finished, often with a nuance of regret, relief, or surprise.
featuredTranslation: I completely spent all the money.
longerExplanation: This adds emotional weight to the completion of an action. It can express sadness/regret (e.g., losing something), relief (e.g., finishing a hard task), or a 'clean break' where nothing remains of the previous state.

sentenceExamples.en: I completely forgot the appointment (regret).
I've gone and finished all my homework (relief/completion).
My friend ended up going back to their hometown (sadness).

name: V-(으)ㄹ 정도로
briefDescription: Used to express the degree or intensity of an action or state by comparing it to another situation.
featuredTranslation: I was so sad to the extent that tears came out.
longerExplanation: This structure sets a 'limit' or 'boundary' to describe how much something is happening. It translates to 'so [X] that [Y]' or 'to the point where [Y]'.

sentenceExamples.en: I laughed to the point that my stomach hurt.
I sang to the extent that my voice went hoarse.

sentenceExamples.kr: 앞이 안 보일 정도로 비가 와요.
sentenceExamples.en: It's raining so hard you can't see ahead.

name: V-ㄴ/는 척하다
briefDescription: Used to describe someone acting in a way that is different from the truth.
featuredTranslation: Please don't pretend to know.
longerExplanation: Attached to a verb or adjective, this indicates the subject is putting on an act. Often used with adjectives like '예쁜 척하다' (pretend to be pretty) or verbs like '자는 척하다' (pretend to be asleep).

sentenceExamples.en: He pretends to have a lot of money.
I pretended not to see and passed by.
Don't pretend to be busy.

name: V-(으)ㄹ까 봐(서)
briefDescription: Expresses that the subject did something as a precaution because they were worried about a certain outcome.
featuredTranslation: Worrying that I might be late, I took a taxi.
longerExplanation: The first clause describes a future event the speaker fears, and the second clause describes the action taken to prevent it or the state resulting from that fear.

sentenceExamples.en: I brought an umbrella worrying that it might rain.
I'm worried that I might fail the exam.
I stayed quiet worrying that I might be noisy.

name: V-(으)ㄹ 리가 없다
briefDescription: Used to strongly deny the possibility of something happening or being true.
featuredTranslation: There is no way he would lie.
longerExplanation: This is a strong expression of disbelief. It literally translates to 'there is no reason/logic for [X].' It is often used when the speaker has strong trust in someone or knows a fact that contradicts a claim.

sentenceExamples.en: There's no way that rumor is true.
There's no way it's already finished.
It's impossible that he doesn't know.

name: V-(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다
englishMeaning: Cannot help but V / No choice but to
briefDescription: Used when there is no other option or alternative but to perform a certain action.
featuredTranslation: I had no choice but to do it alone.
longerExplanation: This double negative structure ('cannot [do] outside of [X]') emphasizes unavoidable necessity. It often suggests a bit of resignation—that the situation forced the speaker's hand.

sentenceExamples.en: Since it's raining, we have no choice but to cancel.
I was so hungry I couldn't help but eat.
There is no other way but to work hard.

name: V-자마자
briefDescription: Indicates that the action in the second clause happens immediately after the action in the first clause.
featuredTranslation: As soon as I arrived home, I contacted him.
longerExplanation: This is used for immediate chronological sequences. Unlike '-고 나서', which just means 'after', '-자마자' emphasizes that there was zero delay between the two actions.

sentenceExamples.en: As soon as I open my eyes, I look at my phone.
As soon as class ended, I went to the cafeteria.
As soon as I graduated, I got a job.

name: V-는 바람에
briefDescription: Used when an unexpected or sudden event in the first clause causes a negative result in the second clause.
featuredTranslation: Because the car broke down, I was late.
longerExplanation: This 'because' is strictly for negative outcomes. It usually implies that the cause was unintentional, sudden, or out of the speaker's control. You cannot use it for positive results.

sentenceExamples.kr: 갑자기 비가 오는 바람에 옷이 젖었어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Because it suddenly rained, my clothes got wet.
Because I was in such a rush, I left my wallet behind.

sentenceExamples.kr: 눈이 많이 오는 바람에 길이 막혀요.
sentenceExamples.en: Because of the heavy snow, the roads are blocked.

name: V-아/어 봐야
briefDescription: Used to say that even if you perform a certain action, the result will be useless or won't change.
featuredTranslation: Even if you go now, it's useless.
longerExplanation: This is a grammar of futility. It often pairs with '소용없다' (useless) or negative outcomes to show that the effort mentioned in the first clause is in vain.

sentenceExamples.en: Even if you regret it now, it's already too late.

sentenceExamples.kr: 아무리 설명해 봐야 이해하지 못할 거예요.
sentenceExamples.en: No matter how much you explain, they won't understand.

sentenceExamples.kr: 혼자 고민해 봐야 답이 안 나와요.
sentenceExamples.en: Even if you worry about it alone, you won't find an answer.

name: V/A-나 마나
briefDescription: Indicates that the result is obvious or the state is fixed, so doing the action makes no difference.
featuredTranslation: Doing that work is pointless.
longerExplanation: It literally means 'whether you do it or don't do it.' It is used when the outcome is so certain that performing the action is a waste of energy.

sentenceExamples.kr: 이 영화는 보나 마나 재미없을 거예요.
sentenceExamples.en: Whether you watch this movie or not, it's going to be boring.

sentenceExamples.kr: 물어보나 마나 그는 안 간다고 할 거예요.
sentenceExamples.en: No need to ask, he'll say he's not going.
The result is obvious without even looking.

name: V-는 길에
briefDescription: Indicates that an action occurs while the subject is in the middle of going somewhere.
featuredTranslation: I bought coffee on the way to school.
longerExplanation: This is used for actions that happen as a 'side task' while moving toward a destination. It is often used with motion verbs like '가다' (go) or '오다' (come).

sentenceExamples.en: I'll stop by the mart on my way home from work.

sentenceExamples.kr: 집에 오는 길에 우연히 친구를 만났어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I met a friend by chance on my way home.
I mailed the letter while on my way to the bank.

name: V/A-(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라
briefDescription: Used to add more information to a statement, showing that something has two or more characteristics or actions.
featuredTranslation: Not only is he kind, but he is also smart.
longerExplanation: This is an additive connector. Note that the nuance must be consistent: you usually add two positive things or two negative things, not one of each.

sentenceExamples.en: The weather is not only hot but also humid.

sentenceExamples.kr: 한국어는 말하기 어려울 뿐만 아니라 쓰기도 어려워요.
sentenceExamples.en: Korean is not only hard to speak but also hard to write.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그 식당은 맛없을 뿐만 아니라 비싸요.
sentenceExamples.en: That restaurant is not only untasty but also expensive.

name: V-(으)려던 참이다
briefDescription: Used when the speaker was already planning or about to do an action at that very moment.
featuredTranslation: I was just about to call (when you called).
longerExplanation: This structure expresses that an intention was already formed and the action was imminent. It is very commonly used when someone else suggests an action that you were already going to do, often preceded by '마침' (coincidentally/just).

sentenceExamples.en: I was just about to head out anyway.

sentenceExamples.kr: 마침 배가 고파서 밥을 먹으려던 참이었어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I was just about to eat because I was hungry.
Just as I was about to start my homework, a friend arrived.

name: V-기 위해서
englishMeaning: In order to V / For the sake of V
briefDescription: Used to express a clear goal, purpose, or intention for performing a certain action.
featuredTranslation: I work hard in order to succeed.
longerExplanation: This is a formal and clear way to express purpose. For nouns, you use 'N-을/를 위해서'. When used with verbs, it emphasizes the determination of the speaker to reach the stated goal.

sentenceExamples.kr: 한국에 가기 위해서 돈을 모으고 있어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I am saving money in order to go to Korea.
I exercise every day to maintain my health.
I got a certificate in order to get a job.

name: V-는 대로
englishMeaning: As soon as V / According to V
briefDescription: Doing something immediately after another action, or according to a certain manner. Similar to: -자마자 (No. 98).
featuredTranslation: Please let me know as soon as it finishes.
longerExplanation: This has two main uses: 1) Time: performing an action the instant another finishes (similar to -자마자). 2) Manner: following a specific plan, word, or state (e.g., 'as you wish' or 'as planned').

sentenceExamples.en: I will call you as soon as I arrive.
Please come quickly, just as you promised.
Please say everything exactly as it comes to mind.

name: N-에 달려 있다
briefDescription: Used to show that a result or outcome is determined by a specific factor or noun.
featuredTranslation: The result depends on your effort.
longerExplanation: This structure identifies the deciding factor for a situation. It is often used to emphasize responsibility or the importance of a certain variable in achieving success.

sentenceExamples.en: Whether you pass or not depends on the interview.
It all depends on your mindset.

sentenceExamples.kr: 모든 것은 우리 손에 달려 있습니다.
sentenceExamples.en: Everything depends on our hands (is up to us).

name: V-(으)ㄹ 만하다
briefDescription: Indicates that something has enough value, merit, or reason to be done.
featuredTranslation: This book is worth reading.
longerExplanation: This structure is used to recommend something. Even if it's not the best, it implies it is 'good enough' or 'deserving' of the action. It can also indicate that a certain reaction is justifiable (e.g., 'it's understandable that...').

sentenceExamples.kr: 그 영화는 한 번 볼 만해요.
sentenceExamples.en: That movie is worth watching once.
I'm looking for a person who is worth trusting (trustworthy).
That news is enough to be surprising.

name: N-는커녕
englishMeaning: Far from N / Let alone N
briefDescription: Used to emphasize that the current situation is much worse than a basic or expected one.
featuredTranslation: Far from sleeping, I couldn't even eat.
longerExplanation: This is used to show a strong contrast between an ideal or expected situation and the harsh reality. It implies that if the 'higher' thing (N) is impossible, the 'lower' thing is obviously impossible too.

sentenceExamples.en: Far from being praised, I only got scolded.
Far from being helpful, it's just a hindrance.
Let alone getting married, I don't even have a girlfriend.

name: V-다가 보니까
briefDescription: Used to express a realization or result that occurred while repeatedly or continuously performing an action.
featuredTranslation: By continuously listening, I came to understand.
longerExplanation: This grammar implies that the subject didn't intend for the result initially, but through the process of doing the action in the first clause, they discovered or arrived at the state in the second clause.

sentenceExamples.kr: 한국 드라마를 보다 보니까 한국어를 좋아하게 됐어요.
sentenceExamples.en: While watching Korean dramas, I came to like the Korean language.
While living busily, I ended up losing my health.

sentenceExamples.kr: 혼자 살다 보니까 요리를 잘하게 됐어요.
sentenceExamples.en: While living alone, I became good at cooking.

name: V/A-듯이
englishMeaning: As if V/A / Just like V/A
briefDescription: Used to describe an action or state by comparing it to something else that is similar.
featuredTranslation: I worked just like a machine.
longerExplanation: This creates a comparison or analogy. It is often used to emphasize the intensity of an action or to describe someone's behavior by comparing it to a well-known phenomenon.

sentenceExamples.en: He spends money like water.
Sweat poured down like rain.
As you know (just like you know), I am a student.

name: V/A-는 반면에
briefDescription: Used to describe two contrasting facts or characteristics about the same topic.
featuredTranslation: While there are advantages, there are also disadvantages.
longerExplanation: This structure acts as a logical balance. If the first clause is positive, the second is usually negative (or vice versa), showing the 'two sides of the coin' for a particular situation.

sentenceExamples.kr: 돈은 많이 버는 반면에 스트레스도 많아요.
sentenceExamples.en: While earning a lot of money, there is also a lot of stress.
While being good at reading, I am clumsy at speaking.
While prices are expensive, the service is good.

name: V/A-면서(도)
briefDescription: Used when the second action or state is unexpected or contradictory to the first one happening at the same time.
featuredTranslation: Even while smiling, I was sad.
longerExplanation: Adding '-도' to '-면서' emphasizes the contrast. It highlights that the two states occurring simultaneously are logically inconsistent or surprising (e.g., someone being rich but acting poor).

sentenceExamples.en: Even though he knows, he pretends not to.
Even though he has a lot of money, he is very frugal.
Even though he is tired, he doesn't sleep.

name: V/A-는데(도)
briefDescription: Used when the result in the second clause is the opposite of what is expected from the first clause.
featuredTranslation: Even though it's raining, there are many people.
longerExplanation: This is a concessive connector. It establishes a background in the first clause and then presents a reality that 'defies' that background. '-는데도' is stronger than just '-는데'.

sentenceExamples.kr: 공부를 열심히 했는데도 시험을 못 봤어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Even though I studied hard, I didn't do well on the exam.
Even though I'm full, I keep eating.
Even though it's night, it's bright outside.

name: V/A-는가 하면
englishMeaning: On the one hand... on the other hand
briefDescription: Used to connect two contrasting or diverse facts, showing that multiple situations exist simultaneously.
featuredExample: 잘하는 사람이 있는가 하면 못하는 사람도 있어요.
featuredTranslation: While some people are good, others are not.
longerExplanation: This formal structure is used to describe diversity within a group or situation. It's like saying 'there is [A], but then again, there is also [B]'.

sentenceExamples.kr: 어떤 사람은 고기를 좋아하는가 하면 어떤 사람은 채소를 좋아해요.
sentenceExamples.en: While some people like meat, others like vegetables.

sentenceExamples.kr: 날씨가 맑은가 하면 갑자기 비가 오기도 해요.
sentenceExamples.en: While the weather is clear, it also suddenly rains sometimes.

sentenceExamples.kr: 가격이 싼가 하면 품질이 좋은 것도 있어요.
sentenceExamples.en: While some things are cheap, there are also things with good quality.

name: V/A/N-든지
briefDescription: Used to indicate a choice between options where the selection does not affect the outcome.
featuredTranslation: Either rice or bread, it doesn't matter.
longerExplanation: This structure shows indifference toward a choice. When repeated (A든지 B든지), it means it doesn't matter which one happens. When used with question words (언제든지, 어디든지), it means 'any-'.

sentenceExamples.en: Whether you go or not, do as you please.
No matter what you eat, it will all be delicious.
No matter where you are, I will always support you.

name: V/A-도록
briefDescription: Indicates a purpose, goal, or the limit of time/degree for an action.
featuredTranslation: I sang until my voice was hoarse.
longerExplanation: 1) Purpose: 'I study hard so that I can pass.' 2) Degree/Limit: 'I worked until I was exhausted.' It defines the extent to which the main action is carried out.

sentenceExamples.kr: 모두가 들을 수 있도록 크게 말씀해 주세요.
sentenceExamples.en: Please speak loudly so that everyone can hear.
We talked until the night broke (all night long).
Please prepare so that the food doesn't run out.

name: V/A-ㄴ/는 다기에
briefDescription: Used to state a reason for an action based on something the speaker heard from someone else.
featuredTranslation: Because my friend said they were coming, I held a party.
longerExplanation: This is a combination of indirect speech (-다고 하다) and reason (-기에). You are performing an action because of information reported to you by another source.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그 집이 맛있다기에 한번 가 봤어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Because I heard that place is delicious, I tried going there.
Because they said it would rain, I brought an umbrella.
Because I heard there was a sale, I went to the department store.

name: V-ㄴ/는 길래
briefDescription: A causal connector used when the reason for the subject's action is based on something they saw or experienced. Similar to: -아/어서 (No. 17).
featuredTranslation: Seeing that he was hungry, I gave him food.
longerExplanation: This is very common in spoken Korean. It usually explains the speaker's reaction to an observed situation or another person's state. It is similar to '-아/어서' but emphasizes the external observation.

sentenceExamples.kr: 사람들이 줄을 서 있길래 저도 섰어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Seeing people standing in line, I stood there too.
Seeing that it was pretty, I bought one.
Because I was bored, I watched a movie.

name: V-(으)려면
briefDescription: Used to state a condition or requirement that must be met in order to achieve a specific goal.
featuredTranslation: If you intend to succeed, you must make an effort.
longerExplanation: This is a contraction of 'V-(으)려고 하면'. It sets the goal in the first clause and provides the 'price' or 'instruction' in the second clause.

sentenceExamples.en: If you want to speak Korean well, practice every day.
If you intend to lose weight, you have to eat less.
If you want to take the subway, go this way.

name: V-기만 하다
briefDescription: Used to describe a situation where a subject does nothing else but a specific action.
featuredTranslation: He only talks and doesn't listen.
longerExplanation: This emphasizes the exclusivity of an action. It can imply that the person is ignoring other necessary actions or simply that one specific state is the only thing happening.

sentenceExamples.en: I did nothing but sleep all day.
That child does nothing but cry.
Don't just laugh, try to answer.

name: V-ㄴ 채(로)
englishMeaning: While maintaining the state of V
briefDescription: Used to describe an action that occurs while a previous action's resulting state is still in effect.
featuredTranslation: I fell asleep with the light on.
longerExplanation: This structure focuses on a 'retained state.' One action is finished (the light was turned on), and while that state remains (the light is still on), another action happens (sleeping).

sentenceExamples.en: He came into the room with his shoes on.
I washed my face with my glasses on.

sentenceExamples.kr: 입을 벌린 채로 멍하게 서 있어요.
sentenceExamples.en: He is standing there blankly with his mouth open.

name: V-고도
briefDescription: Used when the result or action in the second clause is unexpected or contradictory to the first completed action.
featuredTranslation: Even after eating that much, are you hungry?
longerExplanation: This is used for surprise or criticism. It highlights that even though action [A] was fully completed, the expected result [B] didn't happen, or an opposite result happened instead.

sentenceExamples.en: Even after doing something wrong, he doesn't apologize.
Even though I saw it, I pretended I didn't.
Even after hearing it, I couldn't believe it.

name: V-는 줄 몰랐다
briefDescription: Used to express surprise or a correction of a previous misconception.
featuredTranslation: I didn't realize he was married.
longerExplanation: This structure is used when the speaker had a different assumption or was completely unaware of a fact. To say 'I thought/knew [X]', you use '-는 줄 알았다'. It is very common for expressing surprise at unexpected news.

sentenceExamples.en: I didn't realize it had already started.

sentenceExamples.kr: 매운 음식을 못 먹는 줄 몰랐어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I didn't know you couldn't eat spicy food.
I didn't realize today was a holiday.

name: V-ㄴ 나머지
briefDescription: Indicates that an extreme state or action led to an unintended negative result.
featuredTranslation: Due to being so nervous, I made a mistake.
longerExplanation: The word '나머지' literally means 'the rest' or 'remainder.' In this context, it implies that the 'remainder' or 'outcome' of an overwhelming emotion or action was a specific negative event.

sentenceExamples.en: I was so happy that I ended up crying.
As a result of overworking, I got sick.

sentenceExamples.kr: 당황한 나머지 아무 말도 못 했어요.
sentenceExamples.en: I was so flustered that I couldn't say anything.

name: V-ㄹ 뿐이다
briefDescription: Used to emphasize that there is no other action or state besides the one mentioned.
featuredTranslation: I was merely looking.
longerExplanation: This is an exclusivity structure. It minimizes the action, often used to show that the speaker's intention was simple or that they had no further power in a situation.

sentenceExamples.en: I merely told the truth.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그는 웃고만 있을 뿐 아무 말도 안 해요.
sentenceExamples.en: He is only smiling and doesn't say a word.

sentenceExamples.kr: 제가 할 수 있는 것은 기다리는 것뿐이에요.
sentenceExamples.en: The only thing I can do is wait.

name: V-았/었어야 했는데
briefDescription: Used to express regret or a missed obligation regarding a past event.
featuredTranslation: I should have slept early yesterday.
longerExplanation: This structure combines the necessity form (-어야 하다) with the past tense and the background connector (-는데). It implies that the action didn't happen, and the speaker feels sorry or regretful about it.

sentenceExamples.en: I should have studied harder; it's a shame.
I should have brought an umbrella; I got wet.
I should have told the truth back then.

name: V/A-더라고(요)
briefDescription: Used to recount a past event or state that the speaker personally witnessed or experienced.
featuredTranslation: I observed that the Jeju sea was really beautiful.
longerExplanation: This is a 'discovery' grammar. You are telling someone else about something you personally saw, felt, or realized in the past. It adds a nuance of personal testimony to the statement.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그 영화 직접 보니까 정말 슬프더라고요.
sentenceExamples.en: I watched the movie myself, and it was really sad.
I met my friend yesterday, and they were very busy.
I tried eating it, and it was spicier than I thought.

name: V/A-다던데
briefDescription: Used to recall something heard from another source and use it as background for a suggestion or question.
featuredTranslation: I heard it will rain tomorrow, take an umbrella.
longerExplanation: This is a contraction of '-다고 하던데'. It is frequently used when you want to suggest something to someone based on rumors or information you've gathered from the news or other people.

sentenceExamples.en: I heard Korean food is delicious, please recommend some.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그 사람이 곧 회사를 그만둔다던데 사실이에요?
sentenceExamples.en: I heard he's quitting the company soon; is that true?
I heard this exam is very difficult, so I'm worried.

name: V-자(고) 하다
briefDescription: Used to report a suggestion made by the speaker or someone else to do something together.
featuredTranslation: My friend suggested we eat together.
longerExplanation: This is the indirect reported speech for the propositive form (-자). It translates to 'He/I suggested that we [X]'. It is used to relay invitations or collective plans.

sentenceExamples.en: I was the one who suggested watching a movie first.
The teacher suggested that we meet again tomorrow.
Should I suggest that we go on a trip together this weekend?

name: V-는 통에
briefDescription: Indicates a reason for a negative result, usually involving a chaotic or noisy situation. Similar to: -는 바람에 (No. 99).
featuredExample: 소음이 심한 통에 잠을 못 잤어요.
featuredTranslation: Due to the heavy noise, I couldn't sleep.
longerExplanation: Similar to '-는 바람에', but '-는 통에' specifically emphasizes that the cause was a 'disturbance' or a 'hectic' environment. It is almost always followed by a result that the speaker finds annoying or difficult.

sentenceExamples.en: Because the kids are making such a racket, I can't think straight.

sentenceExamples.kr: 전화가 계속 오는 통에 일을 못 했어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Because the phone kept ringing, I couldn't get any work done.

sentenceExamples.kr: 비가 쏟아지는 통에 옷이 다 젖었어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Because of the pouring rain, my clothes got completely wet.

name: N-에 의해서
englishMeaning: By means of N / Through N
briefDescription: A formal way to express the cause, agency, or method of a certain action.
featuredTranslation: This work was proceeded with by means of experts.
longerExplanation: This is a formal, often written structure. In passive sentences, it identifies the agent (the person or thing) that performs the action. It is frequently seen in news reports, academic papers, and official documents.

sentenceExamples.kr: 법에 의해서 처벌을 받을 수 있습니다.
sentenceExamples.en: You can be punished according to (by means of) the law.
It was decided by means of a vote.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그 소설은 유명한 작가에 의해서 쓰였습니다.
sentenceExamples.en: That novel was written by a famous author.

name: V/A-아/어서야
briefDescription: Used to show that a state or action was finally achieved only after a difficult condition was met.
featuredTranslation: Only by making this kind of effort can you succeed.
longerExplanation: The particle '-야' adds strong emphasis to the condition. It implies that the result in the second clause is not easy to reach and requires the specific action in the first clause as a strict prerequisite.

sentenceExamples.en: I only arrived home after it became 11 PM.

sentenceExamples.kr: 직접 먹어 봐서야 그 맛을 알게 됐어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Only after trying it myself did I come to know the taste.
Only after becoming a parent did I understand my parents' hearts.

name: V/A-(으)ㅁ (Nominalizer)
briefDescription: Turns a verb or adjective into a noun for formal writing, titles, or lists.
featuredTranslation: Fast development is necessary.
longerExplanation: Unlike '-기' (which is used for active nominalization), '-(으)ㅁ' is used to turn a verb into a 'state' or 'fact' noun. It is common in official forms, diaries, and written announcements.

sentenceExamples.en: The fact that he is the culprit was revealed.
Classes are cancelled tomorrow (written notice).
Met a friend yesterday (diary style).

name: V-았/었더라면
briefDescription: Used to imagine a past situation that is different from what actually happened.
featuredExample: 그때 그 말을 안 했더라면 좋았을 거예요.
featuredTranslation: It would have been good if I hadn't said those words then.
longerExplanation: This is the counterfactual past conditional. It is almost always followed by a clause expressing regret or an imagined positive outcome like '-았/었을 것이다' or '-았/었을 텐데'.

sentenceExamples.en: If I had studied more, I would have passed.

sentenceExamples.kr: 조금만 더 일찍 왔더라면 그를 만날 수 있었어요.
sentenceExamples.en: If you had come just a little earlier, you could have met him.
If the weather had been good, we would have gone on a picnic.

name: V/A-다가는
briefDescription: Used as a warning that a continuous action will lead to a negative consequence.
featuredExample: 그렇게 빨리 운전하다가는 사고가 날 거예요.
featuredTranslation: If you keep driving that fast, you'll have an accident.
longerExplanation: This structure warns the listener. It takes a current, ongoing behavior and projects a dark or dangerous future result if that behavior doesn't stop.

sentenceExamples.en: If you keep playing around, you'll fail the exam.
If you keep being a picky eater, you could harm your health.

sentenceExamples.kr: 그렇게 돈을 쓰다가는 거지가 될 거예요.
sentenceExamples.en: If you keep spending money like that, you'll become a beggar.

name: V-(으)ㄹ 지경이다
englishMeaning: To be on the verge of V
briefDescription: Used to emphasize an extreme state by saying it is almost at the point of a certain action.
featuredTranslation: I was so tired I was on the verge of collapsing.
longerExplanation: This is a hyperbolic expression. '지경' means 'a boundary' or 'a situation.' You are saying you are so deep in a state that you are right on the edge of the verb happening.

sentenceExamples.en: I'm so hungry I'm on the verge of dying (starving).
It's so noisy I'm on the verge of going crazy.
I waited so long my eyes were about to pop out.

name: V-는 데다가
briefDescription: Used to add information that reinforces the same vibe or direction as the first clause. Similar to: -(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 (No. 103).
featuredExample: 날씨가 추운 데다가 바람도 많이 불어요.
featuredTranslation: In addition to the weather being cold, the wind blows strongly.
longerExplanation: Similar to '-을 뿐만 아니라', but '-는 데다가' feels more like stacking evidence. If the first clause is negative, the second should be negative to show how things are 'piling up'.

sentenceExamples.en: In addition to being kind, he is also capable.
The roads are blocked, and on top of that, it's raining.
The food is untasty, and in addition, it's expensive.

name: V/A-ㄴ/는 다는 것이다
briefDescription: Used for formal statements of fact, conclusions, or emphasizing the main point.
featuredTranslation: The most important thing is that one makes an effort.
longerExplanation: This is a concluding structure used in essays or speeches. It wraps up a complex idea into a singular 'fact' or 'truth' for the listener to focus on.

sentenceExamples.en: The problem is the fact that there is no time.
The core point is the fact that we are together.
The point of what he said is that it's a lie.

name: V-는 척 / 체하다
briefDescription: A formal variant used to describe someone feigning an action or state.
featuredTranslation: Please don't pretend not to know.
longerExplanation: '-체하다' is an exact synonym of '-척하다' but is considered slightly more formal or literary. Both describe behaving in a way that hides the truth.

sentenceExamples.en: He pretends to be all that (acts conceited).
I read a comic book while pretending to study.
I passed by, pretending not to have seen it.

name: V/A-더니
briefDescription: Used to describe a change, contrast, or result based on something the speaker observed about a third person or environment.
featuredTranslation: It was cold in the morning, but now it's warm.
longerExplanation: This grammar is unique because it connects a past observation with a present reality. It can show contrast (was [A], now [B]), or cause and effect (did [A], so now [B]). Note: it is rarely used for the first person ('I').

sentenceExamples.en: My brother studied hard, and (as a result) he passed.
It rained yesterday, but today it's clear.
The child was crying, but suddenly he is laughing.

name: V-(ㄴ/은/는) 거나 마찬가지이다
briefDescription: Used when a situation is so close to a certain result that the difference is negligible.
featuredExample: 거의 다 했으니 이제 끝난 거나 마찬가지예요.
featuredTranslation: Since I'm almost done, it's practically finished.
longerExplanation: This is used for figurative equality. Even if the state hasn't 'technically' been reached, for all intents and purposes, it is treated as though it has.

sentenceExamples.en: If it's like this, it's as good as new.
He is practically the same as family to me.

sentenceExamples.kr: 거짓말을 하는 것은 죄를 짓는 거나 마찬가지입니다.
sentenceExamples.en: Lying is practically the same as committing a sin.

name: V/A-(ㄴ/은) 탓에 / 탓이다
englishMeaning: Because of / Due to (the fault of)
briefDescription: Used to blame a negative result on a specific cause.
featuredExample: 비가 많이 온 탓에 행사가 취소됐어요.
featuredTranslation: The event was canceled because of the heavy rain.
longerExplanation: While '-기 때문에' is a neutral reason, '탓' specifically carries the nuance of 'blame' or 'fault.' You only use this when the outcome is bad and you want to point a finger at the cause.

sentenceExamples.en: Because of (the fault of) oversleeping, I missed the train.

sentenceExamples.kr: 성격이 급한 탓에 실수를 자주 해요.
sentenceExamples.en: Due to my hasty personality, I make mistakes often.
That is all my fault.

name: V-기 마련이다
briefDescription: Used to state a universal truth or an inevitable natural outcome.
featuredTranslation: If you try hard, you are bound to succeed.
longerExplanation: This structure expresses that something is a matter of course. It's like saying 'this is how the world works' or 'it is an unavoidable rule of life.'

sentenceExamples.en: When winter goes, spring is bound to come.
Everyone is bound to make mistakes.
If you commit a crime, it is only natural to be punished.

name: V-기 나름이다 / N-나름이다
englishMeaning: It depends on (how you do) V/N
briefDescription: Used to show that an outcome changes based on the method, effort, or mindset. Similar to: N-에 달려 있다 (No. 107).
featuredTranslation: Happiness depends on your mindset.
longerExplanation: Similar to '에 달려 있다', but '나름이다' emphasizes that the 'quality' or 'way' something is handled determines the result. It suggests that the power to change the outcome lies in the subject mentioned.

sentenceExamples.en: It depends on how a person does it.

sentenceExamples.kr: 물건도 쓰기 나름이라 오래 쓸 수 있어요.
sentenceExamples.en: Even objects depend on how you use them, so they can last long.
Even food depends on how it's made to be tasty.

name: V-다가
englishMeaning: While doing V... / In the middle of V...
briefDescription: Used when an ongoing action is interrupted or changes to another action.
featuredTranslation: While going to school, I met a friend.
longerExplanation: This structure indicates a 'transfer' of action. You were in the middle of doing [A], but then [B] happened or you switched to doing [B]. It is one of the most essential connectors for storytelling in Korean.

sentenceExamples.en: I fell asleep while watching TV.
It was snowing, but then it changed to rain.
I was eating when I got a phone call.

name: V/A-든지 ... V/A-든지
briefDescription: Expresses that the choice between two or more options doesn't matter.
featuredTranslation: Whether you have time or not, please make sure to come.
longerExplanation: This is the repeated form of No. 116. It emphasizes that regardless of which condition in the list is met, the final outcome or the speaker's request remains the same.
